assumed_delays.hazard: Reporting a share of runs 'met in time' built on assumed fence and door delay times will be read as a real protection level although it mostly reflects the assumed numbers.

single_path.hazard: Evaluating only one approach path and one target door overstates protection, because physical-protection practice evaluates the weakest path.

catch_rate.hazard: The gate result is circular: the share of fictitious pickups stopped is essentially the assumed catch probability, so the simulation adds nothing but the queueing cost.

mm1_queue.hazard: A single-guard first-come-first-served gate with uniform service times misses real effects such as appointment windows, bunching of arrivals and a second lane, so queue figures are unrealistic.

nuisance_only.hazard: Comparing alarm policies on nuisance alarms alone hides the real risk of verify-first: slower response when the alarm is a real intrusion.

verifier_reliability.hazard: Assuming a drone or robot dog always correctly clears a nuisance alarm ignores verification errors in wind, rain, darkness or foliage.

evac_no_fire.hazard: An evacuation model without a hazard, blocked exits, crowding at doors or missing persons gives only a best-case muster time.

guard_coupling.hazard: Operations run separately miss their coupling: a guard at a gate check or on an alarm is not available for an intrusion at the same time.

no_night.hazard: Running every operation in daylight with full sensor ranges misses the hours when most warehouse burglaries happen.

dual_use_timeline.hazard: Publishing a protection timeline with barrier delays and the share of runs not met in time could help someone plan an intrusion at a real facility.
